title: Weight-loss drugs show signs of slowing biological aging, say drugmakers
gist: Eli Lilly and Novo Nordisk reported at a longevity conference that GLP-1 drugs slowed molecular aging-clock readouts by roughly two to three years versus placebo (up to 4 years for a heart-protein clock), boosting the aging-clock field and the longevity thesis for GLP-1s, though benefit in healthy people is unproven and ARPA-H is funding a $38 million test.

insights.claim: Lilly and Novo Nordisk found that overweight or diabetic patients on GLP-1 drugs had reduced biological age versus placebo on aging clocks, with an overall difference of around two to three years, though results varied widely by clock type and organ.
insights.speaker: Antonio Regalado
insights.so_what: Company-reported data suggesting GLP-1s act on aging biology; extends the GLP-1 addressable market narrative into longevity.
insights.quote: Both companies found that overweight or diabetic patients taking the drugs, called GLP-1s, had reduced biological age compared to those taking a placebo

insights.claim: Novo drew blood from 10,052 people, half on drug and half on placebo, and measured proteomic clocks; it saw aging slowdowns of as much as 4 years for a clock based on heart proteins.
insights.speaker: Antonio Regalado
insights.so_what: Largest dataset yet in this area; organ-specific effects point to cardiovascular benefit.
insights.locator: As part of its study, Novo took blood draws

insights.claim: Lilly's smaller study of tirzepatide used epigenetic clocks and found that for the most part molecular time moved more slowly for people on the drug, with Lilly's Kevin Duffin saying all clocks tell a consistent story of age reduction but not a 30-year reversal.
insights.speaker: Antonio Regalado
insights.so_what: Second independent clock type and drug point in the same direction, though the study was smaller.
insights.quote: All the clocks are telling a consistent story that we’re seeing a reduction in age

insights.claim: Steve Horvath, credited with inventing aging clocks, called a two-year effect pretty strong and said the data could be evidence that GLP-1 drugs are geroprotectors that slow or possibly reverse biologic aging.
insights.speaker: Antonio Regalado
insights.so_what: Credible academic framing legitimises the longevity use case.
insights.quote: Two years is a pretty strong effect, in my book

insights.claim: Harvard biologist Vadim Gladyshev, who assisted Novo, said semaglutide is an anti-aging drug in an unhealthy population but that no one knows for healthy people.
insights.speaker: Antonio Regalado
insights.so_what: The healthy-population market remains unproven; the thesis is not yet a general longevity drug.
insights.quote: In an unhealthy population, I do think it’s an anti-aging drug

insights.claim: Horvath is not ready to take GLP-1s himself and sees insufficient evidence of benefit for skinny people, and side effects including muscle loss are a reason the drugs might not help most people.
insights.speaker: Antonio Regalado
insights.so_what: Side effects limit use in healthy cohorts; watch for muscle-preservation combination therapies.

insights.claim: ARPA-H put $38 million in January into a Texas study of whether semaglutide has anti-aging effects in healthy people over 60, measuring cognition, mobility and sensory acuity, and aims to help define a regulatory pathway for anti-aging drugs; answers could emerge in a year or two.
insights.speaker: Antonio Regalado
insights.so_what: A key catalyst: regulatory pathway for aging as an indication and the first controlled data in healthy older adults.
insights.locator: This past January, a US agency, ARPA-H

insights.claim: Novo's Aguayo-Orozco declined to say whether a reasonable person should start taking semaglutide for anti-aging, saying he is not a physician.
insights.speaker: Antonio Regalado
insights.so_what: Companies are avoiding off-label longevity claims for now.
insights.quote: I am not a physician. I cannot answer that question,

insights.claim: GLP-1s are the best-selling drugs in the world, with Lilly's tirzepatide (Mounjaro, Zepbound) topping the list at more than $36 billion in revenue last year and Novo's semaglutide a close second.
insights.speaker: Antonio Regalado
insights.so_what: Establishes the revenue base on which any longevity indication would build.
insights.locator: The molecules have become the best selling drugs

insights.claim: The studies are a major boost for aging-clock makers because clocks now show a drop in age with drugs having broad, well-demonstrated benefits, which had been uncertain as true biomarkers.
insights.speaker: Antonio Regalado
insights.so_what: Validation of aging clocks as biomarkers may help longevity biotech trial design and funding.
insights.quote: The clock people have been pushing for a decade to get this kind of study done
insights.locator: The studies are also a huge boost

insights.claim: Insilico Medicine's Alex Zhavoronkov argues humanity is entering a new era of longevity medicines, noting an experimental Insilico lung drug reversed aging-clock signals, and said he himself microdoses tirzepatide and semaglutide.
insights.speaker: Antonio Regalado
insights.so_what: Promotional longevity advocacy; indicates off-label experimentation among longevity community.
